title: Hemodynamics, Thrombosis and Shock
summary: Clots, emboli, edema and the failure of circulation.

lessons.title: Edema and Congestion

levels.kid:
Your blood vessels are like garden hoses carrying water around your body. Tiny hoses called **capillaries** are a little leaky on purpose, so food and water can get to your cells.

Usually the body sucks most of that water back in, so everything stays balanced.

But sometimes too much water leaks out and stays in the wrong place. Then a part of the body gets puffy. That puffiness is called **edema**. If you press on puffy ankles, your finger can leave a little dent!

Edema can happen when the heart is tired, when the kidneys or liver are sick, or when there is a bump or bite. Doctors look for the reason and fix it.
levels.hs:
About 60% of body weight is water, and most of it sits inside cells. The rest is outside cells, in the blood and in the spaces between cells (**interstitial fluid**). **Edema** is extra fluid in the interstitial space.

Fluid movement across capillaries depends on two forces, called **Starling forces**:
- **Hydrostatic pressure**: blood pressure inside the capillary pushes fluid out.
- **Oncotic pressure**: proteins in blood, especially **albumin**, pull fluid back in.

Normally a little more fluid leaves than returns, and the **lymphatic vessels** carry the extra away.

Edema happens when this balance breaks:
- **Higher hydrostatic pressure**: heart failure or a blood clot in a leg vein backs blood up.
- **Lower oncotic pressure**: too little albumin, from liver disease (not made) or kidney disease (lost in urine, nephrotic syndrome) or malnutrition.
- **Leaky vessels**: inflammation, burns, allergic reactions.
- **Blocked lymphatics**: after surgery that removes lymph nodes, or parasitic infection.
- **Salt and water retention**: kidney failure.

**Congestion** is related but different: blood pools in vessels because it cannot drain. Left heart failure congests the lungs, causing **pulmonary edema** and shortness of breath. Right heart failure congests the liver and legs.

Edema in the brain is especially dangerous because the skull cannot expand.
levels.college:
**Starling's equation**: net filtration = Kf [(Pc − Pi) − σ(πc − πi)], where Kf is the filtration coefficient, P hydrostatic and π oncotic pressures, and σ the reflection coefficient for proteins.

**Transudate vs exudate**: transudates (low protein, low specific gravity) result from altered hydrostatic or oncotic pressures with intact endothelium; exudates (high protein, cells) result from increased permeability. Light's criteria classify pleural effusions as exudative if pleural/serum protein > 0.5, pleural/serum LDH > 0.6, or pleural LDH > two-thirds of the upper limit of normal serum LDH.

**Pitting edema** reflects mobile interstitial fluid; **non-pitting** suggests lymphedema or myxedema (glycosaminoglycan deposition in hypothyroidism).

**Heart failure** edema involves both raised venous pressure and renal sodium retention, as reduced effective arterial volume activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, sympathetic nervous system and ADH. Cirrhosis shows a similar paradox: total body water rises while effective arterial volume is low, due to splanchnic vasodilation.

**Pulmonary edema**: cardiogenic (raised pulmonary capillary pressure) vs non-cardiogenic (ARDS, from alveolar-capillary injury).

**Congestion**:
- Acute pulmonary congestion: engorged alveolar capillaries, alveolar edema.
- Chronic pulmonary congestion: hemosiderin-laden macrophages (**heart failure cells**).
- Chronic passive hepatic congestion: centrilobular congestion and necrosis surrounding central veins, giving the **nutmeg liver** appearance; can progress to cardiac cirrhosis.

**Hyperemia** is active (arteriolar dilation, red: exercise, inflammation); **congestion** is passive (impaired venous outflow, blue-red: cyanosis).

**Cerebral edema**: vasogenic (blood-brain barrier disruption; tumors, abscess; white matter), cytotoxic (cell swelling from energy failure; ischemia; gray and white matter), and interstitial (transependymal CSF flow in hydrocephalus).
levels.phd:
The classical Starling model has been revised by the **glycocalyx model**. The endothelial glycocalyx, a gel of proteoglycans and glycoproteins on the luminal surface, acts as the true semipermeable layer. The oncotic pressure that matters is that just beneath the glycocalyx, not in the bulk interstitium, so the protein concentration difference across this layer is larger than predicted. One important consequence is the **'no-absorption rule'**: in most capillaries at steady state there is little or no reabsorption at the venous end; filtrate returns almost entirely via lymphatics. This explains why raising plasma oncotic pressure with albumin infusion has smaller effects on edema than the classical model predicts, and why lymphatic function deserves more attention.

Glycocalyx degradation by inflammation, hyperglycemia, ischemia-reperfusion and even rapid fluid loading (via natriuretic peptide release) increases permeability, a mechanism invoked in sepsis-associated capillary leak.

In the brain, the Starling model needs further modification. The blood-brain barrier, with tight junctions between endothelial cells, is nearly impermeable to small ions such as sodium, so brain water is governed by **osmotic** rather than oncotic gradients. This is why osmotherapy with mannitol or hypertonic saline can draw water out of brain tissue with an intact barrier, while having limited effect in regions where the barrier is broken.

In ischemic stroke, edema evolves in a sequence: cytotoxic edema (no net tissue water gain, just redistribution into cells) then **ionic edema** (sodium moves across an intact barrier through endothelial transporters such as SUR1-TRPM4 channels and Na-K-Cl cotransporters, drawing water) then vasogenic edema as the barrier breaks down, and finally hemorrhagic transformation. Glibenclamide, which blocks SUR1-TRPM4, has been studied to reduce malignant edema, an example of mechanism-driven therapy, with mixed trial results so far.

The discovery of meningeal lymphatic vessels and glymphatic perivascular flow has reopened questions about brain interstitial fluid clearance.
levels.expert:
At the bedside, start with distribution and pitting. Bilateral pitting leg edema: heart failure, liver disease, nephrotic syndrome, venous insufficiency, or drugs (calcium channel blockers such as amlodipine are a classic cause). Unilateral leg swelling: deep vein thrombosis until proven otherwise, or cellulitis, a ruptured Baker cyst, or lymphatic obstruction. Check the jugular venous pressure: high JVP points to the heart or volume overload; a low JVP with edema points to low albumin or a local cause.

**Pulmonary edema** on exam: crackles at the bases, orthopnea, and on chest X-ray, interstitial lines, bat-wing opacities and effusions. Lung ultrasound with multiple B-lines is a fast bedside tool. Acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema is treated by reducing preload and afterload (nitrates, diuretics, non-invasive ventilation) while finding the trigger: ischemia, arrhythmia, valve failure or hypertensive crisis.

**Neurogenic pulmonary edema** follows severe brain insults such as subarachnoid hemorrhage or status epilepticus, attributed to a massive sympathetic surge. Neurosurgeons see it.

**Cerebral edema management** depends on type. Vasogenic edema around a tumor or abscess responds to corticosteroids. Cytotoxic edema after a large stroke or trauma does not, and is managed with head-of-bed elevation, avoiding hypotonic fluids, osmotherapy, controlled ventilation for short-term crises, CSF drainage with an external ventricular drain, and decompressive craniectomy when medical therapy fails. Never give hypotonic fluids to a patient with brain injury; low sodium worsens edema.

**Hyponatremia in neurosurgical patients**: distinguish SIADH (euvolemic, fluid restriction) from cerebral salt wasting (volume depleted, needs salt and fluid), especially after subarachnoid hemorrhage, where fluid restriction can worsen vasospasm-related ischemia.

**Nephrotic syndrome** in a child presents as periorbital puffiness in the morning; check the urine for protein before blaming allergies.

keyPoints: Edema = excess interstitial fluid
Starling forces: hydrostatic pressure pushes fluid out, oncotic pressure (albumin) pulls it in
Causes: high venous pressure, low albumin, leaky vessels, lymphatic block, sodium retention
Transudate = low protein (pressure problem); exudate = high protein (leaky vessels)
Congestion is passive venous pooling; hyperemia is active arterial inflow
Cerebral edema: vasogenic (steroid-responsive), cytotoxic, interstitial

examples.tr: Raised venous hydrostatic pressure plus renal sodium retention cause pitting edema.
Albumin lost in urine lowers oncotic pressure, causing generalized edema.
Chronic passive congestion from right heart failure.

lessons.title: Thrombosis and Virchow's Triad

levels.kid:
When you cut yourself, your blood makes a **clot**, a little plug that stops the bleeding. That is a good clot!

But sometimes a clot forms inside a blood vessel when there is no cut. That is a bad clot. It can block the pipe, like a clog in a sink drain, so blood cannot get through.

A doctor named **Virchow** figured out three things that make bad clots more likely:
- Blood moving too slowly, like sitting still on a long trip.
- A scratched or hurt vessel wall.
- Blood that is extra sticky.

That is why people on long flights are told to get up, walk, and wiggle their legs.
levels.hs:
**Hemostasis** is the normal process that stops bleeding: blood vessels squeeze, **platelets** stick to the injury to form a plug, and **clotting factors** create a mesh of **fibrin** that strengthens it. Afterward, the clot is broken down (**fibrinolysis**).

A **thrombus** is a clot that forms inside an intact blood vessel or the heart, where it should not. In the 1800s, Rudolf Virchow described three factors that promote thrombosis, now called **Virchow's triad**:
- **Endothelial injury**: damage to the vessel lining, from atherosclerosis, smoking, high blood pressure, or surgery. This is the main cause of clots in arteries and the heart.
- **Abnormal blood flow**: stasis (slow flow) or turbulence. Long flights, bed rest, atrial fibrillation (the heart's upper chambers quiver instead of pumping) and aneurysms cause stasis.
- **Hypercoagulability**: blood that clots too easily. Causes include inherited conditions (such as factor V Leiden), cancer, pregnancy, estrogen-containing pills, and recent surgery.

**Arterial clots** are platelet-rich and usually form on ruptured atherosclerotic plaques, causing heart attacks and strokes. **Venous clots** are fibrin- and red-cell-rich and usually form in leg veins (**deep vein thrombosis**, DVT) during stasis.

A thrombus can dissolve, become part of the vessel wall, be broken up and recanalized, or break off and travel as an **embolus**.
levels.college:
**Primary hemostasis**: endothelial injury exposes collagen and von Willebrand factor (vWF). Platelets adhere via glycoprotein Ib binding vWF, become activated, change shape and release granule contents (ADP, thromboxane A2), and aggregate via glycoprotein IIb/IIIa binding fibrinogen.

**Secondary hemostasis**: the cell-based model starts with **tissue factor** exposed at injury binding factor VIIa, generating a small amount of thrombin, which amplifies by activating platelets and factors V, VIII and XI, culminating in a thrombin burst that converts fibrinogen to fibrin; factor XIIIa cross-links it. Calcium and phospholipid surfaces are required.

**Natural anticoagulants**: antithrombin (enhanced by heparin) inhibits thrombin and Xa; protein C, activated by thrombin-thrombomodulin with cofactor protein S, inactivates Va and VIIIa; tissue factor pathway inhibitor; and endothelial prostacyclin and nitric oxide. **Fibrinolysis**: tissue plasminogen activator converts plasminogen to plasmin, which degrades fibrin, producing D-dimers.

**Inherited thrombophilias**: factor V Leiden (most common in people of European descent; factor Va resistant to activated protein C), prothrombin G20210A mutation, deficiencies of protein C, protein S and antithrombin.

**Acquired**: antiphospholipid syndrome (arterial and venous clots, pregnancy loss), malignancy (Trousseau syndrome, migratory thrombophlebitis), heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (paradoxical clotting from antibodies against heparin-PF4 complexes), nephrotic syndrome (antithrombin loss), pregnancy, estrogens, immobilization.

**Morphology**: **lines of Zahn**, alternating layers of platelets/fibrin and red cells, indicate a thrombus formed in flowing blood before death, distinguishing it from a postmortem clot. Mural thrombi form on heart walls after infarction or in aneurysms; vegetations form on valves.

Fates: propagation, embolization, dissolution, organization and recanalization.
levels.phd:
The coagulation cascade's textbook separation of intrinsic and extrinsic pathways reflects test-tube assays (aPTT and PT) more than biology. The **cell-based model** places coagulation on surfaces: initiation on tissue-factor-bearing cells, amplification on platelets, and propagation on activated platelet surfaces where tenase and prothrombinase complexes assemble. The contact pathway (factor XII) is dispensable for hemostasis, since factor XII deficiency causes no bleeding, yet it contributes to pathological thrombosis in animal models. That paradox has made factor XI and XII attractive targets: factor XI inhibitors aim to prevent thrombosis with less bleeding, and several are in late-stage trials, with some mixed results.

**Immunothrombosis** links coagulation to innate immunity. Neutrophil extracellular traps provide a scaffold for platelets and red cells and activate factor XII; monocytes express tissue factor in sepsis. In disseminated intravascular coagulation, widespread activation consumes platelets and factors, leading paradoxically to both microthrombi and bleeding.

Virchow's triad remains remarkably durable, but each arm has been dissected molecularly. In venous thrombosis, stasis in valve pocket sinuses produces local hypoxia, endothelial activation (P-selectin, vWF release from Weibel-Palade bodies), and recruitment of leukocytes and platelets without overt endothelial denudation. Arterial thrombosis depends on high shear: vWF unfolds under shear stress, exposing binding sites for platelet GPIb, which is why arterial clots are platelet-rich and best prevented by antiplatelet agents, whereas venous clots respond to anticoagulants.

Novel thrombotic syndromes have taught lessons: **vaccine-induced immune thrombotic thrombocytopenia** with adenoviral vector vaccines resembled heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (anti-PF4 antibodies) and caused cerebral venous sinus thrombosis; COVID-19 coagulopathy featured endothelial injury and complement activation.

Tumors promote coagulation via tissue factor expression, procoagulant microvesicles and NETs; glioblastoma has one of the highest venous thromboembolism risks of any cancer.
levels.expert:
Every admitted patient gets a VTE risk assessment, because hospital-associated venous thromboembolism is among the most preventable causes of in-hospital death. Mechanical prophylaxis (compression devices) and pharmacologic prophylaxis are chosen by weighing clot risk against bleeding risk.

**Neurosurgery sharpens that tradeoff**. Brain tumor and spinal cord injury patients have very high VTE risk: immobility, malignancy (especially glioma) and surgery hit every arm of Virchow's triad. Yet a postoperative intracranial hemorrhage can be devastating. Typical practice: compression devices from the start, then pharmacologic prophylaxis once imaging and the surgeon judge the bleeding risk acceptable, often a day or so after craniotomy. Know your institution's protocol.

**Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis** is a thrombosis lesson in the brain: headache, seizures, papilledema and sometimes hemorrhagic venous infarcts, in young people, pregnancy, postpartum, with estrogen use or dehydration. Treatment is anticoagulation, even when hemorrhage is present, because the bleeding is caused by venous congestion. Counterintuitive but evidence-based.

**Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia**: platelets fall typically 5-10 days after heparin starts, with new clots. Stop all heparin, including flushes, and start a non-heparin anticoagulant. Do not give platelet transfusions casually.

**When to test for thrombophilia**: rarely in the acute setting, since results are distorted by clot and anticoagulants, and they seldom change management. Consider it with unprovoked clots in young patients, unusual sites (cerebral, mesenteric veins) or strong family history.

**D-dimer**: highly sensitive, poorly specific. A normal value in a low-probability patient (Wells score) helps rule out DVT and PE; a high value proves little after surgery, in pregnancy, cancer or older age.

**Antiplatelet vs anticoagulant**: arteries clot with platelets (aspirin, P2Y12 inhibitors); veins and atrial fibrillation clot with fibrin (anticoagulants). Match the drug to the clot.

keyPoints: A thrombus is a clot inside an intact vessel
Virchow's triad: endothelial injury, abnormal flow (stasis/turbulence), hypercoagulability
Arterial clots are platelet-rich (antiplatelets); venous clots are fibrin/red-cell-rich (anticoagulants)
Factor V Leiden is the most common inherited thrombophilia in people of European descent
Lines of Zahn show a thrombus formed in flowing blood before death
Fates: dissolution, organization/recanalization, propagation, embolization

examples.tr: Stasis in leg veins (Virchow's triad: abnormal flow).
Platelet-rich arterial thrombus on a ruptured atherosclerotic plaque (endothelial injury).

examples.src: Clot in a woman with factor V Leiden taking estrogen

lessons.title: Embolism and Infarction

levels.kid:
Remember bad clots? Sometimes a piece of a clot breaks off and floats away in the blood, like a leaf floating down a stream. That traveling piece is called an **embolus**.

It floats until it reaches a tube too small to fit through. Then it gets stuck and blocks the way.

When blood cannot reach a part of the body, that part does not get oxygen. Without oxygen for too long, that part gets hurt and some of it dies. Doctors call the dead patch an **infarct**.

If it happens in the heart, it is a heart attack. If it happens in the brain, it is a stroke. That is why doctors move super fast to open the blocked tube.
levels.hs:
An **embolus** is any solid, liquid or gas mass carried by the blood to a site away from where it formed. About 99% of emboli are pieces of thrombus (**thromboembolism**). Others include fat (after long bone fractures), air (from IV lines or diving), amniotic fluid (during childbirth), cholesterol crystals, and tumor cells.

Where an embolus lands depends on where it started:
- **Venous emboli**, usually from deep leg veins, travel through the right heart into the **lungs**, causing **pulmonary embolism** (PE). A large PE can cause sudden death.
- **Arterial (systemic) emboli**, usually from the left heart (for example, a clot in atrial fibrillation or after a heart attack) or from plaques in the carotid arteries, travel to the **brain**, intestines, kidneys, spleen or legs.

An **infarct** is an area of tissue death (necrosis) caused by loss of blood supply. Most infarcts come from arterial blockage by thrombus or embolus.

Infarcts come in two colors:
- **White (pale) infarcts**: in solid organs with one blood supply, like the heart, kidney and spleen.
- **Red (hemorrhagic) infarcts**: in loose tissues with two blood supplies (lungs, intestine), in venous blockage, or when blood flow returns to dead tissue.

How badly tissue is damaged depends on how fast the blockage happens, whether backup vessels exist (**collateral circulation**), and how sensitive the tissue is to low oxygen. Neurons die within minutes; skin and muscle survive much longer.
levels.college:
**Pulmonary embolism**: most arise from proximal deep veins of the legs (iliac, femoral, popliteal) rather than calf veins. Consequences scale with size: most small emboli are clinically silent; medium emboli may cause pulmonary infarction only when bronchial circulation is compromised (lungs have dual supply, so infarction is uncommon and usually wedge-shaped and hemorrhagic); massive emboli or a **saddle embolus** at the pulmonary artery bifurcation cause acute right ventricular failure, obstructive shock and death. Recurrent small emboli can cause chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension. **Paradoxical embolism**: a venous clot crosses into the systemic circulation through a patent foramen ovale or septal defect, causing stroke.

**Systemic thromboembolism**: about 80% from intracardiac mural thrombi (infarcted left ventricle, dilated left atrium in atrial fibrillation), the rest from aortic aneurysms, plaques, valvular vegetations. Main targets: lower limbs, brain, intestines, kidneys, spleen.

**Fat embolism syndrome**: typically 1-3 days after long bone or pelvic fracture: respiratory distress, neurologic symptoms (confusion) and a petechial rash (often axillary and conjunctival), plus thrombocytopenia and anemia.

**Air embolism**: venous air embolism during neurosurgery in the sitting position (open dural venous sinuses have negative pressure) or via central lines; decompression sickness ('the bends') from nitrogen bubbles.

**Amniotic fluid embolism**: rare, catastrophic; cardiorespiratory collapse and DIC.

**Infarction morphology**: wedge-shaped with apex at the occluded vessel. Coagulative necrosis in most organs; liquefactive in the brain. Timeline in myocardium: no visible change in the first hours, then coagulative necrosis with neutrophils (days 1-3), macrophages (days 3-7, the wall is weakest and at risk of rupture), granulation tissue, then scar by about 2 months.

Determinants of infarct severity: anatomy of supply (dual: lung, liver; end-arterial: kidney, spleen), rate of occlusion, tissue vulnerability (neurons 3-4 minutes, myocytes 20-30 minutes), and oxygen content of blood.
levels.phd:
Infarction biology is fundamentally about the **dynamics of perfusion and tolerance**. In focal brain ischemia, cerebral blood flow thresholds define functional states: below roughly 20 mL per 100 g per minute, synaptic transmission fails (electrical silence); below roughly 10-12, ionic pumps fail and anoxic depolarization ensues. Between these thresholds lies the **ischemic penumbra**, tissue that is electrically silent but structurally viable for a time that depends on residual flow. The penumbra is not static: **spreading depolarizations**, waves of near-complete neuronal depolarization that propagate slowly across cortex, recruit penumbral tissue into the core, especially in brains with poor collaterals. They have been recorded in human patients with subdural electrode strips after hemorrhage and trauma.

Collateral circulation explains striking individual differences. Leptomeningeal anastomoses between major cerebral arteries vary genetically (mouse strain studies identified loci such as Rabep2 controlling collateral number) and decline with age, hypertension and metabolic syndrome. Patients with good collaterals are called 'slow progressors': their core expands gradually, which is why imaging-selected thrombectomy works late for some and not for others. Tissue clock, not only the wall clock, determines salvageability.

The heart has analogous concepts. **Ischemic preconditioning**, in which brief ischemia episodes protect against a subsequent prolonged one, was first shown in dogs in 1986; remote preconditioning (cuff inflation on a limb) showed promise in small studies but failed to improve outcomes in large trials, a cautionary tale for translational medicine. **Microvascular obstruction** after reperfusion (no-reflow), from distal embolization of plaque debris, capillary compression by edema and leukocyte plugging, predicts poor outcomes.

Embolic stroke of undetermined source (ESUS) became a research category when anticoagulant trials (based on the hypothesis that occult atrial fibrillation drives these strokes) failed to beat aspirin. Long-term cardiac monitoring reveals atrial fibrillation in a minority, and atrial cardiopathy has been proposed as a substrate independent of rhythm.
levels.expert:
**Acute stroke is infarction in real time**, and the system is built around speed. The team assesses the deficit (NIH Stroke Scale), gets a non-contrast CT to exclude hemorrhage, then CT angiography to look for a large vessel occlusion. Eligible patients receive thrombolysis within the approved window, and large vessel occlusions go for mechanical thrombectomy, which can be offered up to 24 hours after last known well in selected patients with favorable imaging. A key phrase is **last known well**, not when symptoms were discovered; wake-up strokes are timed from when the person went to sleep unless MRI-based selection is used.

**Malignant middle cerebral artery infarction**: massive edema peaks over the first days, causing midline shift and herniation. Early decompressive hemicraniectomy in selected patients reduces death substantially; survivors often have significant disability, and the decision involves careful conversations with families about what outcomes the patient would accept.

**Cerebellar infarction** is a neurosurgical emergency in disguise: swelling in the posterior fossa can compress the brainstem and block the fourth ventricle, causing hydrocephalus. Treatment may be a ventricular drain and suboccipital decompression. Watch drowsiness closely.

**Pulmonary embolism**: risk-stratify. A stable patient gets anticoagulation. A PE with shock (massive/high-risk) needs reperfusion: systemic thrombolysis, catheter-directed therapy or surgical embolectomy. Signs of right ventricular strain on echo or CT, and raised troponin, define intermediate risk.

**Venous air embolism in the operating room**: in sitting-position posterior fossa surgery, monitoring includes precordial Doppler or transesophageal echo and end-tidal CO2 (which drops suddenly). Response: flood the field with saline, compress jugular veins, lower the head, aspirate through a right atrial catheter if present, and support circulation.

**Mesenteric ischemia**: pain out of proportion to exam in an older patient with atrial fibrillation. Rising lactate is a late sign. Delay kills.

Always ask the embolic question: **where did this come from?** Echo, rhythm monitoring and vessel imaging prevent the next one.

keyPoints: An embolus is a traveling mass; about 99% are thromboemboli

lessons.title: Shock: Types and Mechanisms

levels.kid:
Your heart is a pump, your blood vessels are pipes, and your blood is the water. All three have to work so every part of your body gets oxygen.

**Shock** is when not enough blood and oxygen reach the body's parts. It is not the same as being surprised!

Shock can happen if:
- You lose lots of blood or water (the tank is low).
- The heart pump is too weak.
- The pipes get too wide and floppy, often from a bad infection or a big allergy.
- Something blocks the pipes.

A person in shock may feel cold, look pale, breathe fast and feel confused. It is an emergency, so call for help right away.
levels.hs:
**Shock** is a state where the circulation fails to deliver enough oxygen to tissues. Cells switch to anaerobic metabolism, producing **lactate**, and organs begin to fail. Low blood pressure is common, but shock can start before pressure falls.

Four main types:
- **Hypovolemic**: not enough volume. Causes: bleeding (trauma, GI bleeding) or fluid loss (severe vomiting, diarrhea, burns). Skin is cold and pale.
- **Cardiogenic**: the heart pump fails, most often after a large heart attack. Also arrhythmias and valve failure.
- **Distributive**: blood vessels dilate widely, so the 'tank' becomes too big for the blood available. Causes: **sepsis** (the most common), **anaphylaxis** (severe allergy) and **neurogenic shock** (spinal cord injury). In early sepsis the skin may be warm.
- **Obstructive**: something blocks blood flow: a big pulmonary embolism, **tension pneumothorax** (air under pressure in the chest) or **cardiac tamponade** (fluid squeezing the heart).

The body fights back with **compensation**: the heart beats faster, vessels to skin and gut tighten, and the kidneys hold onto salt and water. If shock continues, compensation fails, and damage becomes irreversible.

Warning signs: fast heart rate, fast breathing, low blood pressure, cool clammy skin (except early sepsis), little urine and confusion.

Treatment depends on the type: fluids and blood for hypovolemia, antibiotics and fluids for sepsis, epinephrine for anaphylaxis, and fixing the blockage in obstructive shock.
levels.college:
Oxygen delivery (DO2) = cardiac output × arterial oxygen content. Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume; mean arterial pressure ≈ cardiac output × systemic vascular resistance (SVR). Shock types map onto these variables:

- **Hypovolemic**: low preload (low CVP and wedge pressure), low CO, high SVR.
- **Cardiogenic**: high filling pressures, low CO, high SVR.
- **Obstructive**: low CO, high SVR; filling pressures depend on the site (tamponade equalizes diastolic pressures; PE raises right-sided pressures).
- **Distributive**: low SVR, usually normal or high CO after resuscitation, low filling pressures initially.

**Neurogenic shock** (cord injury, usually above T6) is distinctive: loss of sympathetic outflow causes hypotension with **bradycardia** and warm, dry skin, unlike the tachycardia of other types. Do not confuse with spinal shock, the temporary loss of reflexes below an injury.

**Stages**: non-progressive (compensated: baroreceptor reflex, catecholamines, RAAS, ADH), progressive (anaerobic metabolism, lactic acidosis, loss of arteriolar tone, microvascular pooling) and irreversible (widespread cell injury, lysosomal enzyme release, myocardial depression).

**Morphology**: shock causes injury across organs: acute tubular injury in kidneys, diffuse alveolar damage (ARDS) in lungs, centrilobular necrosis in liver, stress ulcers and ischemic bowel, adrenal hemorrhage (Waterhouse-Friderichsen in meningococcemia), and in the brain, **watershed infarcts** at border zones between major arterial territories, plus laminar necrosis of vulnerable cortical layers and selective loss of hippocampal CA1 and cerebellar Purkinje cells.

**Septic shock** (Sepsis-3): sepsis requiring vasopressors to maintain MAP at or above 65 mmHg with lactate above 2 mmol/L despite adequate fluid. Pathogenesis: PAMPs and DAMPs trigger cytokine release, nitric oxide-mediated vasodilation, capillary leak, DIC, mitochondrial dysfunction and immunosuppression.
levels.phd:
The traditional view of shock as a macrocirculatory problem has expanded to include **microcirculatory and cellular failure**. Sublingual videomicroscopy studies in septic patients show heterogeneous capillary perfusion, with stopped vessels adjacent to flowing ones, that can persist after blood pressure is restored; the loss of **hemodynamic coherence** between macro- and microcirculation explains why normalizing pressure does not always rescue organs. Glycocalyx shedding, leukocyte and platelet adhesion, red cell deformability loss and microthrombi all contribute.

At the cellular level, sepsis features **cytopathic hypoxia**: mitochondria fail to use oxygen even when delivered, related to nitric oxide inhibition of cytochrome oxidase, PARP activation consuming NAD+, and mitochondrial damage. Interestingly, organ dysfunction in sepsis often occurs with little cell death on histology, and organs recover in survivors, prompting the hypothesis that organ failure is partly an adaptive hibernation-like downregulation of metabolism.

Lactate is not simply a marker of anaerobic metabolism. In sepsis, epinephrine stimulates beta-2-adrenergic Na+/K+ ATPase activity in muscle, accelerating aerobic glycolysis and producing lactate even with adequate oxygen, while impaired hepatic clearance contributes. Lactate is also a fuel shuttled between tissues, including heart and brain. Its prognostic value is robust; its interpretation as purely 'oxygen debt' is not.

Hemorrhagic shock science has driven trauma practice. Early resuscitation with large crystalloid volumes worsened coagulopathy, acidosis and edema; recognition of the **lethal triad** (hypothermia, acidosis, coagulopathy) and acute traumatic coagulopathy (driven by protein C activation and endothelial injury) led to **damage control resuscitation**: permissive hypotension until hemorrhage control (except in traumatic brain injury), balanced blood product ratios, early tranexamic acid, and damage control surgery. Whole blood has re-emerged, partly informed by military experience.

In the brain, autoregulation normally keeps flow constant across a range of pressures; injured brain loses this, so cerebral perfusion becomes pressure-passive and hypotension becomes directly harmful.
levels.expert:
**Recognize shock early**: tachycardia, a rising respiratory rate, mottled skin, prolonged capillary refill, low urine output and confusion appear before the systolic pressure collapses, especially in young people, who compensate until they suddenly crash. The shock index (heart rate divided by systolic pressure) above roughly 1 is a red flag in trauma.

**Find the type fast**. Bedside ultrasound (the RUSH-style approach) looks at the pump (ventricular function, pericardial effusion with tamponade), the tank (IVC size, free fluid in the abdomen or chest) and the pipes (aortic aneurysm, DVT). Combine with the exam: raised JVP plus hypotension suggests cardiogenic or obstructive causes; flat neck veins suggest hypovolemia or distributive shock.

**Treat by type**:
- Hemorrhage: stop the bleeding (direct pressure, tourniquet, surgery, interventional radiology), give blood products early, reverse anticoagulants, prevent hypothermia.
- Sepsis: cultures, antibiotics within the first hour, fluid resuscitation guided by response, norepinephrine as the first-line vasopressor, source control.
- Anaphylaxis: intramuscular epinephrine immediately; antihistamines and steroids are adjuncts, not substitutes.
- Tension pneumothorax: decompress without waiting for imaging; tamponade: pericardiocentesis; massive PE: reperfusion.
- Cardiogenic: revascularize ischemia, inotropes, mechanical support in specialized centers.

**The neurosurgical angle**: in traumatic brain injury, a single episode of hypotension markedly worsens outcomes, so permissive hypotension does NOT apply; guidelines target higher systolic pressures. Cerebral perfusion pressure = MAP − ICP, so shock and raised ICP attack the same equation. In acute spinal cord injury, neurogenic shock needs vasopressors with chronotropic action and atropine for bradycardia, and many centers target a higher MAP for the first days to protect cord perfusion.

**Never attribute hypotension in a head-injured adult to the head injury alone** until bleeding elsewhere (chest, abdomen, pelvis, long bones) is excluded. An isolated head injury rarely causes shock in adults, except terminally.

keyPoints: Shock = inadequate tissue oxygen delivery; lactate rises
Four types: hypovolemic, cardiogenic, distributive, obstructive
Distributive shock (sepsis, anaphylaxis, neurogenic) has low vascular resistance
Neurogenic shock: hypotension with bradycardia and warm skin
Compensation: tachycardia, vasoconstriction, salt and water retention; then progressive and irreversible stages
In brain injury avoid hypotension: CPP = MAP − ICP
